Hello, 

I’ll budge in here a little bit and add additional details. This has been no recent change - we have had these checks for years silently in the background.

The extra prevention that we started applying is based on *profiling:* it means we started seeing a lot of irregularities (and especially payment problems and fraud reports) from certain customer data points such as device, email etc and, as prevention, we added a score to the customer to indicate risk as it is customer based profiling (not business itself). Now if the customer would just have one risky factor then it would not introduce any additional actions. Sadly, we see these customers have reached the limit of different small risks (into significant risks) and as a result, we ask the customer to confirm they are legitimate through verification. This is just a one-time procedure to ensure 1) Bolt can alleviate the risk 2) the customer to receive a future seamless experience. The customer is NOT blocked, certain services are risky for them to receive based on the many risks that have accumulated and if they proceed with verification, they will have a much more frictionless life going forward (as we can confirm who they are and trust them).

Sadly, we have no information easily attainable at the checks' stage about the CC company type (or actually any billing type other than CC vs Postpaid) → these topics are currently on hold due to internal team restructuring (as is every bigger change) and will require significant dev work to be continued. However, as I have aforementioned then this is not about the company itself but the particular business user has significant risk due to their ‘customer group and details' being flagged in the association. 

*So what can we do?* 

If you notice that many of your local customers are unwilling to proceed with verifications then we can consider lowering the ‘risk’ per flag in your region. However, as always this will make life easier for those with malicious purposes or bad history customers. Remember, these flags are indicated due to irregularities on a larger scale. 

I would *not* even consider removing the flags and risk completely as they make a very important line in our already very limited fraud defences. We can consider adding business level ‘securities’ → Good business = customer gets _further_ additional risk alleviation in your region. But the problem here is that we have very limited information on the business, the checks done and confirming the business to be trusted. And to be very frank then human company verification is not 100% effective and, understandably so, as the fraudsters are often highly educated on how they can fool agents - some things will never be visible to the naked eye. While in the long term we are planning on adding helpful information to the signup checks: fraud signaling, for example, and a VIP trusted business flag that can be controlled by local teams → these are all things that require engineering and the business cases to do so will always be very insignificant in comparison to other topics. Hence, sadly no quick fixes on how we approach the cases, and tools at our current availability will have to be used instead. 

We also have had cases that INSIDE the business, certain users are misbehaving and misusing Bolt. So the business can be good, but some of its users are very risky on their own. 

You have also mentioned reluctance by customers - would you have even more information? Perhaps we can explain or ‘sell’ it to them better - verification is an important protection (and customer security) method for Bolt. “I wouldn’t share my ID with providers like Bolt” - _Do you feel like our verification services are not secure?_

*_Automated decision-making if you are a user of the rental services_*



*What personal data do we process?*



When you use our Bolt rental electric scooters, we process your personal data collected via the sensors of the scooter to ensure you are using our services in a safe manner. The type of data we process from scooters includes geolocation data, vehicle speed, motor power (including voltage and throttle level) and driving style information (including sudden braking or skidding). This data is used to identify reckless driving events, ie. skidding, abrupt braking, tandem riding, bad parking and collisions. 



*How do we process your personal data?* 



Our internal monitoring system tracks each event that occurs whilst a user is using the scooter, assigns it a certain weight, then calculates an overall score for reckless driving and issues a warning once the user reaches a certain score threshold. The total score of the user is the sum of the reckless events over the last five rides.



If we detect any potentially dangerous behaviour then we will issue the user with a warning in the app to encourage them to refrain from using the scooter in a certain way. There are three levels of warnings: 



# *first warning* - informs the user about the risks of misbehavior; 
# *second warning* - limits the speed of the scooter until the overall user score improves; and 
# *third warning* - temporarily suspends the user from the service. The user is able to contest the suspension by contacting our Customer Support Team for further information as to why their account was suspended.



For safety considerations, we cannot disclose the exact thresholds that trigger our warnings to prevent users from abusing the system.

There are a lot of notes, insights, screenshots and data files in the links above.

All these investigations together produced the following findings:

# Event loop lag across multiple fraud checks can run between 50-100 ms regularly
# Calls to Targeting API, Redis, etc that use a timeout of 100-150 ms, get a higher error rate due to event loop lag
# Generating profiles locally has not provided us with answers as to _where_ these timeouts come from. 

Right now the PINT team has not taken a look, and we don’t have other more granular data to use for profiling (cc Continuous Profiling / Grafana Pyroscope initiative from PINT).

Recommendations are:

* Increase horizontal scale when event loop lag gets too big and affects our error rates
* Tune timeouts to make sure that event loop lag is accounted for - Targeting uses a 200 ms timeout for Redis.
* Make it possible to give a “partial answer” when there are timeouts
* Given that these spurious errors mean that a fraud check will error out, there can be a tangible cost for each fraud check. Maybe we can calculate it

ivan.honchar: Current investigation results.
The problem happens when:
1. User uses applepay/googlepay (also known as mobile wallet payments instruments)
2. User has debt from previous orders
3. User does several attempts to start an order (by attempt I mean "user clicks confirm/start order button")
The problem has several components:
1. Commerce `.../microMobility/preAuthorise` is called twice per user attempt (not 100% sure; to be confirmed)
    a. or only fraud check is called twice :thinking_face: . I need to check it
2. Fraud changes decision between attempts
*Why `.../microMobility/preAuthorise` is called twice?*
I guess it is due to applepay/googlepay payment instrument. Each payment with these payment instruments should be confirmed by user.
So, the 1st call to `/preAuthorise` returns pre-auth amount. Mobile app asks user to confirm payment. User confirms it. Payment system makes authorization.
After that mobile app / rental backed calls `/preAuthorise` again.
Likely, the same may happen with bank card as well if 3DS is requested
Note: it is interesting, but it works differently in Rides. There is no a 2nd call in Rides, when applepay/googlepay is used. It is interesting how it is implemented in Rides :thinking_face:

*Why Fraud changes decision between attempts?*
Every payment authorization attempt costs money, even failed attempts. Fraud together with Payments implemented a feature to reduce number of failed attempts.
So, there is a counter on Fraud side, which counts number of attempts to start an order (actually, number of times fraud check is called by the user within the last hour).
When the user reaches configured threshold, Fraud starts to return REJECT_TOP_UP decision to avoid/stop authorizations.

*Quickfix*
• Fraud Analysts will increase the threshold mentioned above. Thus, users will need to make more attempts until they reach the threshold => less chances to reach it
*Potential solutions*
• Avoid multiple calls per user attempt
    ◦ Understand how Rides implemented the flow in similar case. Maybe MicroMobility should use the same approach
    ◦ or cache and return the same decision by Fraud in case input request wasn't changed
• Fix the counter me

Considering it's so urgent, I was able to review the data protection clause. Overall, we cannot accept it, as Bolt would be considered an “operator” under the POPIA, which is the equivalent of “data processor” under the GDPR. I left a pushback comment and I can also suggest to supplement it with the following message:

{quote}“When providing services to its business customers, Bolt acts as a "responsible party" under the POPIA, which is equivalent to the term of “data controller” under the GDPR. Our General Terms and Conditions for Bolt Business Section 4 states explicitly that Bolt and the business customer maintain their independent data controller roles for personal data processing. Bolt fully assumes responsibility for its processing activities and adherence to applicable laws, including the GDPR. This covers areas such as engaging subprocessors, implementing necessary security measures, and establishing data retention periods.

When a business customer`s employee or any data subject uses Bolt Business services for a ride, they are treated as a regular user of the Bolt Rider App. The experience of these business users is identical to that of regular users, except for the availability of an alternative payment option (Bolt Business) and an additional ride category (Business Ride). This may result in a scenario where, if a business customer deactivates and removes a business user's account, this individual will lose access to an alternative payment option (Bolt Business) and an additional ride category (Business Ride). However, they will continue to be a customer of Bolt, which means Bolt will keep processing their personal data unless this individual decides to request data deletion or the data retention period specified in Bolt`s privacy notices expires. In practical terms, this means that the personal data provided by business customers is used to match newly added business users with the accounts of standard users. Individuals remain in control over their data.

Additionally, as there had been a contractual relationship with the business customer, some personal data received from the business customer may be required for solving any dispute that may arise from the agreement with the business client. Deleting all personal data on the request of business customers may deprive both Bolt and the individual from the opportunity to defend or substantiate their claims in the event that any claims should arise. Therefore, some personal data will be retained by Bolt as a data controller for the above stated purpose unless the individual decides to [request|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/data-subject/] data deletion or the data retention term provided by the law (limitation period for possible claims) expires, as outlined in the applicable Bolt`s[ privacy notices|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/].

Please note that the notion of controllership in our arrangement is cemented by the [EDPB Guidelines 07/2020|https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-072020-concepts-controller-and-processor-gdpr_en] on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. Specifically, p. 27 para. 82 demonstrates this via “Example: Taxi service”. While Bolt operates as an online platform rather than providing taxi services directly, the example still effectively clarifies the logic underpinning the controller relationship.

We appreciate your attention and trust that this explanation has clarified any concerns or questions you may have.”{quote}

The following tickets, all relate to the same problem statement: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-4909|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-4909|smart-link], [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-8190|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-8190|smart-link] [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-15556|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-15556|smart-link] [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-15579|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/WD-15579|smart-link]. {panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Problem Statement:* The overall problem statement lies in the data at source, and the processing logic that occurs within Telema system. When invoices are processed, any codings are aggregated (either by human, or auto). Telema applies their “rounding” logic which adds a new rounding line, with a few cents - example of this has been written very well here in the previous comment on this ticket. In high-level, when Telema makes a reduction of a line amount by a few cents, and instead applies that to rounding, when data is passed to Workday - a re-calculation is performed on the line level that actually the tax amount due on the *line* of the invoice is higher/lower and this calculates a different tax amount, resulting in the incorrect total invoice account, further resulting in incorrect payment.

Telema eFlow module is designed to work as ENTREC - [https://telema.com/telema-eflow/|https://telema.com/telema-eflow/|smart-link] . This means that the Telema system produces a GL entry to be booked directly into a GL accounting system, whereas we are further processing the invoice as a supplier invoice into our Workday ERP system. This is not fit for us as an organisation. 

The problem does not lie here in the integration, or the Workday system. The problem lies in source. Every supplier invoice we receive (with some minor exceptions) should be a digital copy of the physical document. The same principle applies for e-Invoices/EDI. The data that is being sent, goes 1:1 between systems. Data should not be aggregated at source system, with additional rounding logics applied. 

*The problem therefore lies in the source data in Telema, and their calculation logic creating ENTREC.* 

Further problem statement are creating because of this, including but not limited to: 

* Incorrect invoice payment amount
* Tax reporting having to manually remove rounding lines
* Incorrect VAT amount calculated 
* Aggregated data not being sufficient for spend analysis 
* Lack of Workday Functionalities being able to be utilised due to Telema logics
{panel}



I am going to close this ServiceDesk ticket, but I will refer you to *two* Finance Platform Jira tickets, which are both detailing the technical solutions, on which you are able to track progress, we will notify you of any changes that we are due to implement, engage you in testing, and the agreed operating procedure. 



The executive decision which I take the responsibility for, is that we must NOT over-customize any integrations, and must fix the problem at source. To take a pragmatic approach, we will take a two-step process, which I will detail below:

Hi [~accountid:60f2a71843c956007065f2ad] 🙂 First, I’d like to give some context on how GDPR requests from users (officially called “Data Subject Requests or DSRs) are handled.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*DSR process overview*
{panel}

* At Bolt, all requests under GDPR from all types of users (rider, driver, passenger, etc) are handled following the DSR process.
* Data deletion request is considered a DSR, and all the requirements under GDPR apply to handling data deletion requests, including the timelines of handling these requests (i.e. 30 days under law), when it can be refused, what should be included into it.
* We have the data deletion process description in Beehive Knowledge base: [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360010217173|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360010217173]

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Next steps on this specific case*
{panel}

* Since the request has come from a driver *indirectly* and via a fleet, we have two options:
** either to request the driver to submit the request to us directly via customer support or via DSR form available [*here*|https://bolt.eu/ro-ro/privacy/data-subject/]
** to request the fleet to provide us with an authorization that would let the fleet submit a data erasure request on behalf of the driver
** Alternatively, we can ask the fleet to share the driver’s details with us and we would contact the driver directly.

➡️ [~accountid:60f2a71843c956007065f2ad] can you contact the fleet (or ask CS to contact the fleet) and ask them to share the driver’s details so we can contact him?



❗ What is very important - all data deletion requests have to be handled in line with our process, meaning that we cannot refuse these requests in full or by default. When the driver contacts us, we will handle the request in line with the GDPR.

*5.1*. *5.2.* Although Bolt is neither the manufacturer or seller of Goods, nor provider of the delivery services and is not responsible for respective goods or services, *Bolt* will *try to facilitate an amicable* solution and *may provide a refund or Balance in respect of the affected Goods or the delivery, if Bolt has reasonable cause to believe that the complaint is justified.*

* Clause 5.2 clearly states that even though Bolt is not a manufacturer or seller of goods or a provider of delivery services, Bolt is facilitating amicable solution and may, at its own discretion, provide a refund for affected goods if the complaint is justified, but is not obliged to do so. Hi [~accountid:6052891960d39e006f72f0f0] from Commerce Legal I have no concerns with this. From Fin. Reg. side, also cashback to Bolt Balance is OK. 

However, I just want to make sure we do not give cashback for certain things, as the Card Schme Rules have limits on the things a customer can get a cashback for (or limits to what a Merchant can give cashback for). 

Cashback is generally allowed only for purchases of tangible goods, not for standalone services or intangible goods. For example, service-oriented merchants like consultants or professionals may not be authorized to offer cashback. 

In the EU, certain regulated products, such as pharmaceuticals, alcohol, and tobacco, may have restrictions on cashback offerings due to stringent control over sales and distribution. So I would like to avoid giving/offering cash back for these kind of products. 

Moreover, and as complement to the Card Scheme Rules, the PSD2 encourages measures to ensure the security of transactions, which may include limits on the amount of cashback dispensed to prevent misuse or fraud.

As far as we do not offer cashback for regulated products, and there is a limit on the cashback amount (and limit on how many cashbacks maybe as well) that a customer can receive, from Commerce Legal we are good.

## *Clarifications of whether any of these countries (other than Malaysia)* *_legally require_* *this feature to be implemented*; and

{color:#ff5630}*Why these Qs are important*{color}: 

* We have encountered various cases recently where other individuals are able to gain access to a user’s account through using a +recycled phone number+ to validate their access. This raises a lot of privacy issues, including possible personal data breaches. Bolt as a company is still in the process of finding a solution to this issue, and until one is found, we will continue to encounter cases of other individuals unintentionally gaining access to user accounts.

* As such, we need to understand: (1) the countries we are dealing with here (given that in some countries we are already applying strategies to mitigate the recycled phone number issue); and (2) whether we can find a way to avoid / mitigate the risk of any compromised account displaying the personal information of emergency contacts to an individual that has unintentionally gained access to that account using a recycled phone number.

Looking at this from a higher level, {color:#4c9aff}+*we would ideally want to resolve the recycled phone number issue BEFORE the Trusted Contact Feature is rolled out*+{color}, as this would be the most effective means of dealing with the risks discussed above. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others. SUPPLIER INVOICE APPROVALS HAVE BEEN CONFIGURED IN BOLT2, WITH MULTIPLE TRIES, AND OPTIONS:

Overall, invoice approvals should occur in Workday but UX is KEY, dashboard, and it is important that invoice approvals are *submitted* by *AP SPECIALIST* in Workday wherever possible.

Invoice approvals need to link to *invoice costing allocation* that has been submitted and various rules built out from that logic. 

The invoice approval route, can go through two separate routes (with 1a, and 1b), flowchart pending: 

# PO Invoice - we have a PO reference submitted on the supplier invoice. 
## Workday PO - If the invoice has a Workday related purchase order (non-grocery spend) then the AP Specialist should book the invoice, against the PO. Info pending on SOP. This will then trigger 3-Way matching rule, and if MATCHED, invoice approved and goes for payment. If EXCEPTION then the PO buyer responsible for resolving that relevant transaction.
## WMS PO - for Bolt Market related invoices, the volumes and complex grocery operating logic has determined that it is best to *send* those invoices into WMS system (by logic tbc) via RaaS (report as a service). Data received by WMS to perform 3WM in their system and return via API a result of invoice matched/not matched nad APPROVED/DENIED. SOP to follow.
# Non-PO Invoice
## For non-po invoices, which still make up majority of our invoices - we may not have the relevant PO/contract in place. AP may need to book it and input the *COST INITIATOR* to be the relevant “Approver” field on the invoice. This will be the first approver. Then dependant on cost center(s) and other dimensions booked on invoice, system to route to approves based on the policy in place. AP will be able to track the approvals, the queues for budget owners and we will be able to send nudges/reminders for them.



For spend approvals via WD the following items are key for success:

# User Experience: The UX aspects in the screens from Workday seem outdated, therefore to give the users as much easy to use experience, and SPLIT SCREEN IS MUST! 
# Dimension Simplification: Initiative by [~accountid:712020:dd196f63-fc49-4d36-a37f-98d0ff95f347] to have a simplified logic that allows , Business, AP, Procurement, Controlling and other interested teams to have a good logic to follow and understanding how costings are booked, how they transfer into actuals and the impact.
# Financial Dashboard: budget owner dashboard to: potentially show budget (not currently available) show QoQ spend, show split by relevant country/city/market/business lines. Overall: cost center manager dashboard, for ENHANCED user experience from telema.
# Slack Integration: this is a MAYBE for approve/deny directly from slack, but again UX for split screen may be more difficult. HOWEVER… maybe link to WD supplier invoice, then approve/deny via slack? maybe. 
# Realistic Policy: the legal policy in place does not reflect actual approvals in Telema… so, a REAL policy - risk based and business focused needs to be in place.

Hi [~accountid:60d82cdd8a72bd006c366e1d] , there are several judgements of Polish courts pursuant to which a “fixed-term” agreement cannot be terminated by notice without a reason as it is contrary to the concept of a “fixed-term” agreement, i.e. if a term is fixed, then the agreement should not be terminated before the term for which it was concluded.

*Risk*: If Bolt wishes to terminate the agreement before 3 years by 6-month notice, then the LL may claim that this right is unenforceable and Bolt is obliged to lease the premises until the 3-year period elapses.

*Solution*: 

# Defining specific reasons in which Bolt may terminate the fixed-term contract, e.g. cessation of Bolt Market’s activity in Warsaw, not generating specific income from the specific store for 3 consecutive months, etc. Please note that even if we indicate that Bolt can terminate the agreement due to “valid reasons”, it might be considered as not enough or
# Accepting the “risk” that Bolt will be obliged to lease the premises for 3 years, without option to exit.

Please note that the above risk will occur only in case it is raised by the LL, i.e. it does not apply by virtue of law, etc.

Sharing some of my thoughts on this as well.


While there are no specific grounds in Bolt T&Cs for refusing to make the payment, this can essentially be derived from the general law, in particular [the German Civil Code section 134|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_bgb/englisch_bgb.html#:~:text=Section%20134%0AStatutory,a%20different%20conclusion.] which states that “A legal transaction that violates a statutory prohibition is void, unless the statute leads to a different conclusion.” This means that if making the payment would cause Bolt to violate a particular sanction - the purpose of which is to prohibit such transactions - then the fleet has no grounds for demanding the payment as the transaction would be illegal and therefore void. Furthermore, finding other ways to make the payment would be considered as circumventing the sanction which is also prohibited.

Currently, the only catch is that we do not know what exact sanction the bank is referring to and we have no way to confirm its existence and content. However, as the bank has already revealed to Bolt that they have identified a sanction hit, then there is no reason to assume the bank is wrong and Bolt should have enough reason to believe that by making the payment it would be in violation of the law, potentially even committing a criminal offence (circumventing the sanction).

Please note that for future reference, +drivers and fleets should not be informed of the fact that there has been a potential sanction hit on them+. As explained in [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba] ‘s [overview|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1-AWysyV30X9AffQFv2avdd4YagXAMcMYPdbJkRIoGXE/edit], this could be considered as “tipping-off” and it might have a negative impact in Bolt’s relation with the banking partner. Instead, they should simply be informed that Bolt is unable to complete the transaction due to the bank and the fleet should contact the bank for further information.

Dear Inmaculada López Pinilla 

*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 

 

Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *15 June 2024.*

 

After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 

 

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software.Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail,  we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

 

We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Trip history from March 2024*

 

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our Privacy Policy at [https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|https://bolt.eu/en/legal/|smart-link]  , which includes further information about:

* The categories of personal data we process;
* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;
* The criteria we use to determine how long to retain personal data;
* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

 

*Your rights* 

 

In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

 

 

Yours sincerely,

 

Bolt

*** Where the reported user is the driver and the event is determined to be *homicide* or *rape*, the Assessment Tool will disregard the No Response field and suggest the original consequential action.
*** Where the reported user is the rider and the event is determined to be one of the events from the *physical/sexual assault* or *criminal activity Groupings*, the Assessment Tool will disregard the No Response field and suggest the original consequential action.

With the new risk review update, it is has been clarified how to close cases of no response: 

* _If the reported user does not respond to the allegation for High and Significant Risk Type Events, tick_ *_Yes_* _for the_ *_No Response_* _field in the Assessment Tool._
** _Ticking this field as_ *_Yes_* _alters the Assessment Tool’s suggested_ *_Consequential Action_* _for events where the_ *_Event Confirmation_* _field is chosen as_ *_Cannot Be Confirmed_*_, instructing that the investigative suspension should not be lifted. The case should be reviewed once the reported party gets back to us. The following exceptions apply in the Assessment Tool:_
*** _Where the reported user is the driver and the event is determined to be_ *_homicide_* _or_ *_rape_*_, the Assessment Tool will disregard the No Response field and suggest the original consequential action._
*** _Where the reported user is the rider and the event is determined to be one of the events from the_ *_physical/sexual assault_* _or_ *_criminal activity Groupings_*_, the Assessment Tool will disregard the No Response field and suggest the original consequential action._

Also, it is now possible to amend the tool outcome once the user gets back: 

|_Re-open (Edit) and Amend_|_By clicking_ *_Re-open (Edit)_* _after the tool has been submitted as completed, it will erase the_ *_Yes_* _response to_ *_Has The Assessment Been Completed?_* _question and push the form to a re-opened state, making it editable._
_Once the form has been filled out, save it by clicking_ *_Amend_* _without re-triggering any workflows._|

Hope this helps 🙂

I discussed this matter with the Privacy team, and this is what I got:

At the moment we *can* “delete” accounts with scheduled blocks. 

The main point here is that we do not actually “delete” the accounts of drivers in fact, we just change the status. 

When we were discussing the update to the instructions, we advised some OPS and engineers to understand whether changing the status to deleted in Admin would affect any safety investigation block. What we do is that if there is a block, CS team does NOT lift the block and just changes the status of the account to “deleted”. It does not affect anything on our side.

Once Legal & Compliance finishes their work on the deletion guidelines, the PEX team will be ready to adjust the process but currently, this is how it is.

{code:sql}with spot as (SELECT
    a.id,
    a.created as spot_created,
    a.name,
    a.type,
    a.polygon,
    a.deployment_priority,
    a.buffer_radius,
    a.is_deleted,
    --determine centroid of polygon
    ST_Centroid(ST_GeometryFromText(CONCAT('POLYGON((',json_extract_scalar(polygon_raw_json, '$.polygons[0][0].shape') ,'))'))) centroid,
    --beginning of polygon parser--
    coalesce (
    CASE
        WHEN a.buffered_polygon not like '%oly%' then a.buffered_polygon
        ELSE JSON_EXTRACT_SCALAR(a.buffered_polygon_raw_json,'$.polygons[0][0].shape')
    END,
    CASE
        WHEN a.polygon not like '%oly%' then a.polygon
        ELSE JSON_EXTRACT_SCALAR(a.polygon_raw_json,'$.polygons[0][0].shape')
    END) as shape_1
FROM ng_rental.rental_fleet_city_area a
JOIN ng_public.admin_system_city c on a.city_id=c.id
WHERE
    a.polygon_raw_json is not null
  and a.id =4204873
  ),
  users_first_ride_in_grorud as (
SELECT
 o.user_id, min(o.created) first_ride_in_grorud 
FROM ng_rental.rental_order_order o
 JOIN spot
  ON
  (
  ST_Contains(ST_GeometryFromText('POLYGON((' || spot.shape_1 || '))'), ST_Point(o.dropoff_lat,o.dropoff_lng))
  )
  or 
  (
  ST_Contains(ST_GeometryFromText('POLYGON((' || spot.shape_1 || '))'), ST_Point(o.vehicle_lat,o.vehicle_lng))
  )  
where o.city_id=74 and o.created_date between date'2024-06-17' and  date'2024-07-07' and o.state='finished'
group by 1
),
first_rides_in_grorud_and_ever as (
select frg.*, min(o.created) first_ride_ever
from users_first_ride_in_grorud frg
join ng_rental.rental_order_order o on frg.user_id=o.user_id  and o.state='finished' and o.city_id =74
group by 1,2
)
select count(case when first_ride_ever=first_ride_in_grorud then user_id else null end) first_riders,
count(*)
from first_rides_in_grorud_and_ever{code}

Hi Zuza!

Thank you for the ticket. Overall, let me write to you an update on the assessment that we have carried out in our team. The business requirement you have here, is that you process some ADR goods into your warehouse, and you would like to ensure that on the packing list (at time of outbound goods process) you want this to be identified on the list, so a sticker/right shipment can be made.

We have carried out a lifecycle review of the ADR goods process, and it is as follows:

# Goods are ordered via procurement, and delivered to CWH. Goods are received and stocked. If ADR goods, then these may have to be placed with special rules for Health & Safety (BHP). 
# Stock Requests are made to ship those goods out - when that is made, a packing list is generated to pick items, identify which items are ADR, put relevant sticker on shipment and packed pallet.
# When the shipment is booked via Cargoson platform, a button needs to be ticked, to signify it is ADR goods. 
# Courier picks the goods up, and needs to be aware it is an ADR shipment he is carrying, and he is licensed and has the right machinery to operate that. 
# When goods arrive at final destination, they may also be required to store ADR goods differently.

It is important to therefore ensure ALL parts of the ADR parts lifecycle can be automated, and risk can be reduced at every step - enabling the people to do better work and not have to worry about it.

We are going to develop two things, and we can make a decision as to which one is more suiting:

A) *Item Tag* - add an item tag to items, with a TRUE/FALSE whether an item is an ADR good.

B) *Purchase Item Group* - we could create a new PIG, and assign items there. This would therefore make it better for maintenance, and you would always have visibility as to what items are there.

We will be exploring both of these options, but it will be next week at the earliest due to capacities on current activities, and suggesting the options to you before deployment. This will require functional configuration, integration update, and potentially packing list layout change.

ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_payment_problem THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS pp_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_propagated,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS propagated_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback OR co.is_payment_problem OR co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_fraud,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback OR co.is_payment_problem OR co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS fraud_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_untouched,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS untouched_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_we_added,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS we_added_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN (co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) END) AS double),1) AS how_much_we_added_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_we_deducted,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS we_deducted_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN (co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) END) AS double),1) AS how_much_we_deducted_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.partner_price_eur = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS closed_to_zero,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.partner_price_eur = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS closed_to_zero_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_refunds,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS refund_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS refund_sum_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) AND COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_refunds_by_us,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) AND COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS refund_by_us_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) THEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate END) AS double),1) AS refund_by_us_sum_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.uncovered_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS fp_sum_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.reporting_fraud_loss_eur,0)) AS double),1) AS fraud_loss_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS adjusted_sum_eur
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = co.order_id AND o.city_id = co.city_id 
JOIN ng_public.price_review_price_review pr ON pr.order_id = co.order_id AND pr.city_id = co.city_id 
LEFT JOIN ng_public.invoicing_refund_refund_log rl ON rl.system_type = 'ride_hailing' AND rl.order_id = co.order_id AND rl.city_id = co.city_id
WHERE co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('week', -10, current_date) as date)
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND pr.finished_admin_user_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604)
AND TRUNCATE(o.actual_price_eur/o.price_prediction_eur,1) < 2 
--GROUP BY 1--,2,3,4
--ORDER BY 1 DESC{code}

Hi Team - Apologies for the delay on this. Our advice on sharing the DOB information with Wise is below. 

In short, the only material privacy issue is that *there is a compliance risk with sharing this information in terms of transparency*. However, this is not critical and *should not act as a blocker*.

----

+*Legal Justification*+

For context, Bolt can only share this personal information with Wise if it has a specific legal basis for doing so. We have previously discussed that Bolt itself is not subject to a legal obligation to share this data with Wise - rather, it wants to do so in order to ensure that its users get paid as efficiently as possible. It therefore appears that Bolt has a +legitimate interest+ in sharing the data (which is a legal basis recognised by applicable data protection law), and so {color:#36b37e}*has an appropriate legal basis*{color}.

Where Bolt relies on legitimate interest as a legal basis, we should conduct an analysis (known as a ‘+Legitimate Interest Assessment+’) to ensure that this has been properly considered and assessed. This can be handled by myself on the privacy side and is not a blocker to going ahead with the data sharing, and so this is just an FYI.

----

+*Transparency*+

Bolt must at all times make sure that its drivers and couriers are appropriately informed about how Bolt processes their personal information (which includes sharing date of birth information with third parties). Ordinarily, Bolt informs these users through its privacy notices.

Having reviewed the relevant privacy notices for drivers and couriers, {color:#ff5630}*these could be more transparent*{color} with regards to Bolt sharing DOB information in this way (for example, they do not _explicitly_ mention that Bolt processes DOB information, and the legal basis section needs to be expanded to explicitly incorporate Bolt’s legitimate interest in ensuring that drivers / couriers are paid as efficiently as possible (see above)). +This is a compliance risk, but it is not critical+ (and does not act as a blocker to sharing the DOB information) - in the long term the privacy team just needs to ensure that the privacy notices are updated to reflect this. We will handle this from our side.

For completeness, we could address this risk in the short term by sending the riders / couriers some disclaimer wording to notify them that their DOB information is being shared in this way. However, I understand that Bolt typically only chooses this option where the processing activity is high risk (it is not in this case) and it would be feasible / convenient to do so (it would not be in this case), and so to do so here would be disproportionate.

----

+*Contractual Protections*+

Although Bolt ordinarily pushes for its own data sharing agreements, I understand that Bolt has already accepted Wise’s [EU Customer Terms for Card Payments (Business|https://wise.com/eu/legal/wise-card-processing-agreement]), which contains provisions governing transfers of personal data. This agreement characterises the parties as independent controllers, and does not need to contain international data transfer provisions as we are just dealing with Ukraine here. As such, there are {color:#36b37e}*no obvious privacy compliance issues from a contractual perspective*{color}.

However, it is worth flagging for completeness that this agreement requires Bolt to +indemnify+ Wise, but not the other way around, and does not appear to be subject to a cap. This is more of an FYI than anything else.

Hey [~accountid:5b7beb0fc5e21441d0929c5c] ,

Anastasija’s previous comment is correct; {{rider_campaign_compensation}} essentially means the rider discounts that we reimburse back to the driver/fleet in markets where ‘demand incentives netting' is enabled (part of commission netting a.k.a. dynamic commission). This amount is originally compensated to the rider by the driver, and then we return it back to them as a discount from driver’s commission.

If you look at this document [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/4941906594/Fleet+Portal+Earnings+Mapping|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/4941906594/Fleet+Portal+Earnings+Mapping|smart-link] , you can see each record type (such as rider_campaign_compensation) and which earning type they are under - earning type being the list FleetX team shared below). So, according to this documentation, it is under {{EARNING_IN_APP_DISCOUNT}} and/or {{EARNING_CASH_DISCOUNT}} earning types. I am not sure where exactly in the portal FleetX team display these earning types, but according to their documentation ([Earnings Dashboard & Billing Mapping|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/186-SyG4yHevwl6cueKsm8oWuyYG3-oaFCE_7iZGrtDo/edit?gid=0#gid=0] in [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4006904129/Earnings+Dashboard|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4006904129/Earnings+Dashboard|smart-link] ), these are not exclusively displayed, but rather used in the calculation of certain fields in the fleet portal. Namely, {{Vat on revenue in app}}; {{Vat on revenue cash}}; {{Cash Gross Earnings}}; {{Cash In Hand}}; {{Payouts}}.

Main outputs from the chat with the Public Policy team:

🔴 LP is different per city not by our choice or by a decision made in local teams in that region. The UK is highly regulated, each individual City/Borough has its own licence conditions as they have their own council and regulations. For example:

* Return to the operator within 24/48/72 hours
* Return to operator at the earliest opportunity if items found over the weekend.
* Return to the local police station  - On occasion these are also specific police stations
* Return to the council office office

🔴 We keep a record or the Driver ID, Order ID, Rider Profile, where the driver is licensed, the item dropped off, date dropped off, date collected, who collected. We also have photo evidence of the items in which we upload to the NL portal. This is to satisfy the conditions and also ensure if we are audited we have full records and we do not put our licences in jeopardy.

🔴 NL was first introduced in London due to the issues CS was causing with the LP process. We found a easy efficient way to handle lost property without CS getting too involved as they were providing the wrong information to drivers and passengers which would cause issues at the hub. Even with NL we tend to still have CS mistakes which we often have to raise to CS TL’s.

🔴 In 2022 we had 17,976 items reported lost via NL and in 2023 we had 7,110. London has one of the highest lost rates in the UK and the system we use really helps us manage that with the automated correspondence and logs.

:yellow_circle: In regards to having a different form for different cities, UK OPS is not sure why NL has made it this way, it could be because all forms generate automated messages to start the return process so it needs to be separate? 

----

💭 Seems like the NotLost system is more efficient for the market than the global process - both in terms of keeping the relevant data, aligning with regulations and preventing errors.

🎯 *Asked UK OPS to initiate a conversation with NL about why there are different forms for each city to understand further and include me if needed.*

Hi all

Re/ the privacy aspect of the Seamless AI Terms

*Summary:*

The Terms are far from ideal. There are no GDPR provisions on data transfers between controllers, which is not absolutely critical, but adds a lot of uncertainty and legal risks if we *receive* personal data. Additionally, the Terms include requirements for Bolt which we do not usually accept.

On top of that, we will formally need to sign a data protection safeguard - C2C 2021 EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) if we transfer personal data to Seamless AI, as they are US based.

*Details:*

*Transfers from Seamless AI to Bolt*

The Terms lack explicit GDPR data transfer mechanisms and impose limitations on Bolt re data use, ie require Bolt:

* to process data lawfully and only for the purpose of B2B prospecting (generally ok);
* inform Seamless AI if the data provided by them is compromised in a data incident, which includes *suspected* unauthorised access to or misuse, theft, misappropriation or other compromise (which is generally not ok, as we do not want to report ay suspected breaches).

Overall, this is definitely not in line with our standards, but because its a transfer between data controllers, there is no standard form under the GDPR for such transfers, so no explicit breach of law is happening where there is no written safeguards between us.

Virtually, any collaboration procedures under the GDPR are not clarified, which is not formally critical, but adds a lot of uncertainty and legal risks. For example, how will Seamless AI and Bolt collaborate to conduct DPIAs under Art. 35 of the GDPR (Data Protection Impact Assessment), or if there is an inquiry from a regulator.

It will have to be assumed that in the course of the transfer and data processing, Bolt complies with the GDPR and applicable privacy laws for the data transferred, and the same is assumed for Seamless AI + that the data collected by Seamless AI is collected lawfully.

For low risk and low volume transfers, such risks could be acceptable, but with higher volumes and higher sensitivity of the data, the risks will be too substantial to freely proceed, IMO. Its up to the stakeholder to decide if we want to proceed or ensure additional privacy safeguards in this case.

*Transfers from Bolt to Seamless AI*

There is a standard form where the personal data transfer is happening from the EU to the US - EU Standard Contractual Clauses 2021. 

As the service allows Bolt to submit data to Seamless AI upon integration with other platforms (my assumption - Salesforce), we will have to separately request and sign the Standard Contractual Clauses for this use case - to ensure the lawfulness of such data transfers.

The Terms state that where data is submitted by Bolt, it's our responsibility to ensure the lawfulness of such a transfer of such data.

*Appended Privacy Notices/CCPA Notices*

The appended privacy notice/CCPA notice are not relevant for inter-entity transfers, and are generally designed to explain how Seamless AI processes the data that is collects from individuals (ie cookies, scrapped public personal data, employment context, etc).

Summary of the advice:

*Summary:*

The Terms are far from ideal. There are no GDPR provisions on data transfers between controllers, which is not absolutely critical, but adds a lot of uncertainty and legal risks if we *receive* personal data. Additionally, the Terms include requirements for Bolt which we do not usually accept.

On top of that, we will formally need to sign a data protection safeguard - C2C 2021 EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) if we transfer personal data to Seamless AI, as they are US based.

*Details:*

*Transfers from Seamless AI to Bolt*

The Terms lack explicit GDPR data transfer mechanisms and impose limitations on Bolt re data use, ie require Bolt:

* to process data lawfully and only for the purpose of B2B prospecting (generally ok);
* inform Seamless AI if the data provided by them is compromised in a data incident, which includes *suspected* unauthorised access to or misuse, theft, misappropriation or other compromise (which is generally not ok, as we do not want to report ay suspected breaches).

Overall, this is definitely not in line with our standards, but because its a transfer between data controllers, there is no standard form under the GDPR for such transfers, so no explicit breach of law is happening where there is no written safeguards between us.

Virtually, any collaboration procedures under the GDPR are not clarified, which is not formally critical, but adds a lot of uncertainty and legal risks. For example, how will Seamless AI and Bolt collaborate to conduct DPIAs under Art. 35 of the GDPR (Data Protection Impact Assessment), or if there is an inquiry from a regulator.

It will have to be assumed that in the course of the transfer and data processing, Bolt complies with the GDPR and applicable privacy laws for the data transferred, and the same is assumed for Seamless AI + that the data collected by Seamless AI is collected lawfully.

For low risk and low volume transfers, such risks could be acceptable, but with higher volumes and higher sensitivity of the data, the risks will be too substantial to freely proceed, IMO. Its up to the stakeholder to decide if we want to proceed or ensure additional privacy safeguards in this case.

*Transfers from Bolt to Seamless AI*

There is a standard form where the personal data transfer is happening from the EU to the US - EU Standard Contractual Clauses 2021.

As the service allows Bolt to submit data to Seamless AI upon integration with other platforms (my assumption - Salesforce), we will have to separately request and sign the Standard Contractual Clauses for this use case - to ensure the lawfulness of such data transfers.

The Terms state that where data is submitted by Bolt, it's our responsibility to ensure the lawfulness of such a transfer of such data.

*Appended Privacy Notices/CCPA Notices*

The appended privacy notice/CCPA notice are not relevant for inter-entity transfers, and are generally designed to explain how Seamless AI processes the data that is collects from individuals (ie cookies, scrapped public personal data, employment context, etc).

*The stakeholder, considering its 1 way transfer to Bolt and limited scope of the data transfer, decided to proceed without requesting the updates and accepting the risks.*

Hi all

Upon checking the DPA, I can summarise as follows:

* generally, it complies with the GDPR Art. 28 (and supposedly the local UAE privacy laws, as referenced in the document); however, it does not include a list of sub-processors (likely they forgot to include it, I doubt they do not use any sub-processors) + it does not include a list of organisational and technical security measures when processing our data - we usually reference our standard Information Security Code of Practice - [https://bolt.eu/en/security/supplier-requirements/|https://bolt.eu/en/security/supplier-requirements/] as we require the suppliers to comply with it;
* additionally, the DPA does not comply with any of our internal standards for DPAs, and it would be a business decision to proceed in such case. For example, it includes general authorisation for subprocessors (we require specific authorisation), no clear timeline for notification of subprocessors (we require 15-30 days notice), no clear timelines for notifying data subject rights requests (we usually require 3 days notice); limitations on the right to conduct audits, etc.

Overall, considering the above, I would rather request the supplier to accept our own standard DPA template, and insert the description of the processing operations there. Lots try making them sign our template, and see if we get any pushback.

*Meta's Policies on WhatsApp Usage*

# *User Consent*: Meta requires explicit user consent for using WhatsApp as a communication channel. This means users must clearly agree to receive messages via WhatsApp.
# *Clear Opt-in*: The user must actively choose WhatsApp as their preferred communication channel. This can be achieved through a button like "Get code via WhatsApp," but it should be clear and unambiguous.
# *Additional Information*: Providing additional information about what the user is consenting to is crucial. This includes how their phone number will be used and stored, and that they will receive OTPs via WhatsApp.
# *Compliance with Local Laws*: In addition to Meta's policies, we need to ensure compliance with local laws regarding user consent and data protection, which can vary significantly between jurisdictions.


*Recommendations*

# *Explicit Consent Button*: The "Get code via WhatsApp" button is a good start. Ensure that it is prominently displayed and clearly indicates that the user is opting to receive the OTP via WhatsApp.
# *Additional Text/Popup*: It is advisable to include a brief text block or a popup that informs the user about the use of their phone number for WhatsApp messages. This can be something like:

* "By selecting 'Get code via WhatsApp', you consent to receive your OTP via WhatsApp to the provided phone number."

# *Privacy Policy Update*: Our privacy policy should explicitly mention the use of WhatsApp for OTP OR how such data will be handled.


*Example Text for Button and Popup*

* *Button*:
* "Get code via WhatsApp"
* *Popup/Additional Text*:
* "By clicking 'Get code via WhatsApp,' you consent to receive your OTP via WhatsApp to the provided phone number. Learn more about our [Privacy Policy|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/]."


*Legal Compliance in Target Markets*

# *Nigeria (NG)*:

* Nigeria Data Protection Regulation (NDPR) requires explicit consent for data processing. Ensure you have clear opt-in mechanisms and transparency about data use.

# *South Africa (SA)*:

* Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) requires explicit consent and transparency regarding how personal information is used. Make sure your consent mechanism aligns with these requirements.

# *Other African Countries*:

* Data protection laws vary, but the general principle of explicit consent and clear communication applies widely.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*LT government introduced new requirements re criminal data collection*
{panel}

Summary:

* While criminal convictions-related data is not sensitive data under GDPR, additional restrictions apply to it
* LT government approved a new law easing the collection of criminal convictions data
* Guidelines issued by the LT privacy regulator (VDAI) here: [https://vdai.lrv.lt/media/viesa/saugykla/2024/6/6r36kivPWIM.pdf|https://vdai.lrv.lt/media/viesa/saugykla/2024/6/6r36kivPWIM.pdf]
** In short, LT privacy law only regulates *employee* criminal data collection 
** As drivers are not employees, we cannot rely on the new law in Lithuania



{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*When we can collect criminal data on all drivers (foreign and local)*
{panel}

* GDPR applies to Bolt, as we are processing personal data within the EU
* Data about criminal convictions, among other things, can be processed when we have a legal obligation to check this data (as you mentioned before, this obligation is set forth in the Transport Law)
* As I understood previously, we have a legal obligation to ensure that the drivers have impeccable reputation (i.e. nepriekaistinga reputacija in LT).
** Please note (as mentioned in the documents attached by Elina to this ticket) - administrative offence data is not an element to impeccable reputation, so we can only check criminal convictions data
* To my understanding, we only need to check the fact if the driver was convicted or no, so please make sure to not retain the data for a long period of time. It’s suggested to erase any certificates/excerpts from convictions registry asap and not keep them on our systems



{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Checks of foreign drivers*
{panel}

* It’s more of an operational question, however, please note that the same rules apply to the protection of personal data to foreign drivers

+*Automated decision-making if you are a user of the rental services*+

*What personal data do we process?*

When you use our Bolt rental electric scooters, we process your personal data collected via the sensors of the scooter to ensure you are using our services in a safe manner. The type of data we process from scooters includes geolocation data, vehicle speed, motor power (including voltage and throttle level) and driving style information (including sudden braking or skidding). This data is used to identify reckless driving events, i.e. skidding, abrupt braking, tandem riding, bad parking and collisions.

*How do we process your personal data?*

Our internal monitoring system tracks each event that occurs whilst a user is using the scooter, assigns it a certain weight, then calculates an overall score for reckless driving and issues a warning once the user reaches a certain score threshold. The total score of the user is the sum of the reckless events over the last five rides.

If we detect any potentially dangerous behaviour then we will issue the user with a warning in the app to encourage them to refrain from using the scooter in a certain way. There are three levels of warnings:

#  *first warning* - informs the user about the risks of misbehaviour;
#  *second warning* - limits the speed of the scooter until the overall user score improves; and
#  *third warning* - temporarily suspends the user from the service. The user is able to contest the suspension by contacting our Customer Support Team for further information as to why their account was suspended.

For safety considerations, we cannot disclose the exact thresholds that trigger our warnings to prevent users from abusing the system.

We may also use automated decision-making in order to undertake fraud checks which are necessary for us to perform our services, ensure that the services are paid for and ensure the protection of riders from fraudulent transactions on their payment cards.

*_Automated decision-making if you are a user of the rental services_*



*What personal data do we process?*



When you use our Bolt rental electric scooters, we process your personal data collected via the sensors of the scooter to ensure you are using our services in a safe manner. The type of data we process from scooters includes geolocation data, vehicle speed, motor power (including voltage and throttle level) and driving style information (including sudden braking or skidding). This data is used to identify reckless driving events, ie. skidding, abrupt braking, tandem riding, bad parking and collisions. 



*How do we process your personal data?* 



Our internal monitoring system tracks each event that occurs whilst a user is using the scooter, assigns it a certain weight, then calculates an overall score for reckless driving and issues a warning once the user reaches a certain score threshold. The total score of the user is the sum of the reckless events over the last five rides.



If we detect any potentially dangerous behaviour then we will issue the user with a warning in the app to encourage them to refrain from using the scooter in a certain way. There are three levels of warnings: 



# *first warning* - informs the user about the risks of misbehavior; 
# *second warning* - limits the speed of the scooter until the overall user score improves; and 
# *third warning* - temporarily suspends the user from the service. The user is able to contest the suspension by contacting our Customer Support Team for further information as to why their account was suspended.



For safety considerations, we cannot disclose the exact thresholds that trigger our warnings to prevent users from abusing the system.

Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person.

As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, the law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties.  Furthermore, we must point out that we are not required to disclose documents or otherwise provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.

We therefore attach a summary of the relevant communications (insofar as these comprise your personal data), from which certain information has been redacted in accordance with the above.

For information on how we process relevant personal data, we refer you to our privacy notice for drivers ([https://bolt.eu/ro-ro/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/ro-ro/privacy/privacy-for-drivers/?category=rides|smart-link] ), which includes further information about:

* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* The existence and envisaged consequences of any automated decision-making/profiling of personal data; and
* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

*Your rights* 

You have the right to request rectification or erasure of personal data or restriction of processing of personal data concerning you or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 

If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You have the right to complain directly to the appropriate supervisory authority and seek a judicial remedy. If you have any additional questions, please do not hesitate to reply to this message.

Your sincerely,

Bolt Privacy Team

** [~accountid:63da287e790148a18093a774] Did we confirm with Latvian advisors that this means that the company providing “outsourced accounting” service is only obligated to apply the AML law towards persons to whom it offers the accounting service (and not towards all persons to whom it is offering any other services)?

Hey Anastasija,

This is due to how Campaigns team send the bonus records to Billing. Here is another example case we looked into: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02C2SY0MHT/p1716295749936309|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02C2SY0MHT/p1716295749936309|smart-link] 

There are 2 known reasons why this might happen:

# Fraudulent rides / adjustments reduce the amount of a bonus after the bonus amount was granted. This causes the adjustment to look with a negative amount in the app.
# Campaigns team is giving the bonus amount to fleet’s in advance (before the campaign period is completed), and then, at the end of the campaign period, they recalculate and take the amount that wasn’t earned by the fleet/driver back which is displayed as a negative value in the portal/app.

For example, let’s say there is a bonus of 100€ in total. The fleet gets this bonus fully in the beginning of the period. At the end of the period, the calculations show that the fleet is only eligible for 70€. So, campaigns team take the 30€ back, which is then displayed as -30€ in the portal/app.

*It’s the 2nd option for this driver when I look at his daily records (bonus records sent to Billing by Campaigns team).*

!Screenshot 2024-07-14 at 00.46.41.png|width=100%,alt="Screenshot 2024-07-14 at 00.46.41.png"!

This is obviously very frustrating for the driver. I believe it would be better if we just sent one amount at the end of the Campaign period. Hopefully, Campaigns team will work on that.

Previously we had the step for the agents to educate the rider about contacting the driver via the app if less than 24 hours passed since the trip.

However, there is also a self-help article and an automation that tell the rider exactly the same thing.

That’s why it was decided to remove this part from the process and have agents handle all the lost item requests regardless of the timeline to make the resolution more efficient. 

Let me know if you have any questions and have a great week ahead!

* If I remember correctly, you mentioned that we’d ask for administrative offences information only if we have a suspicion of the driver acting inappropriately on our platform (please correct me if I’m wrong)
** I suggest requesting administrative offence data only as a last resort, and we need to have a good reason to do that, meaning that:
*** Our other processes/features do not “catch” the driver and
*** We cannot block the driver for breaches of terms and conditions
** We need to clearly document a process of when we see that we’d need to ask for administrative offences data and what practical use it gives us - please note that even if a Driver had a speeding ticket or parked in a disabled parking space when acting in his personal capacity, we most likely won’t be able to block the driver, as he/she did not make the offence while driving on our platform



*Regarding criminal convictions:*

* While I am not familiar on the “types” of documents that could be received with the criminal convictions certificate, we should apply a general rule and only collect what’s needed for us to make a decision. This means that it’s a business decision to make. I can help you make that decision, but I’d need to receive more details on what types of documents there are.
* Regarding the time period - does it really make sense to require a lifetime proof? To my understanding, based on different crimes, the fact of conviction (i.e. “teistumas”) will only be shown in the criminal convictions record for a certain period of time, based on different statutes of limitation in the Criminal Code (i.e. 20 years for murder, X years for theft, etc.). Having that in mind, I’d suggest making the time period shorter, for example, 5-10 years.
** This will help us avoid collecting excessive data
** In any case, if the status of the driver is a “convict” and if the record is still active, we’d see this information nevertheless.



Also, can you please clarify what you mean by this: “_To proceed further, should we list all rules for asking for this document to be accessible publicly or can we determine internal rules only and document them in, for example, market-specific Safety incidents management process description?“?_

* *_If you’re asking if this should be a global or a local process_* - it should be local; criminal conviction and administrative offence data collection should be assessed based on local laws, so my team would need to do a separate analysis for each market
* *_If you’re asking where should these rules be published_* - as far as it’s clear that it only applies to Lithuania and not other markets (and thus does not create confusion for other teams), it’s up to you where to put it.

APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_cbs,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS cb_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_payment_problem THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_pps,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_payment_problem THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS pp_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_propagated,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS propagated_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback OR co.is_payment_problem OR co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_fraud,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.is_chargeback OR co.is_payment_problem OR co.propagated_chargeback THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS fraud_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_untouched,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS untouched_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_we_added,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS we_added_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) > 0 THEN (co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) END) AS double),1) AS how_much_we_added_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_we_deducted,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST(( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS we_deducted_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN ROUND(CAST((co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) < 0 THEN (co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) END) AS double),1) AS how_much_we_deducted_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.partner_price_eur = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS closed_to_zero,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN co.partner_price_eur = 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS closed_to_zero_ratio,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_refunds,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS refund_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS refund_sum_eur,
APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) AND COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041) AS count_refunds_by_us,
ROUND(CAST(APPROX_DISTINCT(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) AND COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0) > 0 THEN co.id END,0.0041)*1.000/APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS double),3) AS refund_by_us_ratio,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN rl.admin_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604) THEN COALESCE(co.refund_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate END) AS double),1) AS refund_by_us_sum_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.uncovered_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS fp_sum_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM(COALESCE(co.reporting_fraud_loss_eur,0)) AS double),1) AS fraud_loss_eur,
ROUND(CAST(SUM( co.partner_price_eur - o.actual_price_eur - COALESCE(co.tips_amount,0)/co.eur_currency_rate) AS double),1) AS adjusted_sum_eur
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = co.order_id AND o.city_id = co.city_id 
JOIN ng_public.price_review_price_review pr ON pr.order_id = co.order_id AND pr.city_id = co.city_id 
LEFT JOIN ng_public.invoicing_refund_refund_log rl ON rl.system_type = 'ride_hailing' AND rl.order_id = co.order_id AND rl.city_id = co.city_id
WHERE co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('week', -10, current_date) as date)
AND co.order_type = 'rides'
AND pr.finished_admin_user_id IN (3006,3025,6579,12281,15982,11826,15604)
--AND o.actual_duration_in_min/o.pred_duration_in_min < 0.5
GROUP BY 1--,2,3,4
ORDER BY 1 DESC{code}

Bolt retains your data for only as long as necessary for the purposes described above. This means that we retain different categories of data for different periods of time depending on the type of data, the transportation service it relates to, and the purposes for which we collected the data.

*_Automated decision-making if you are a user of the rental services_*

 

*What personal data do we process?*

 

When you use our Bolt rental electric scooters, we process your personal data collected via the sensors of the scooter to ensure you are using our services in a safe manner. The type of data we process from scooters includes geolocation data, vehicle speed, motor power (including voltage and throttle level) and driving style information (including sudden braking or skidding). This data is used to identify reckless driving events, ie. skidding, abrupt braking, tandem riding, bad parking and collisions. 

 

*How do we process your personal data?* 

 

Our internal monitoring system tracks each event that occurs whilst a user is using the scooter, assigns it a certain weight, then calculates an overall score for reckless driving and issues a warning once the user reaches a certain score threshold. The total score of the user is the sum of the reckless events over the last five rides.

 

If we detect any potentially dangerous behaviour then we will issue the user with a warning in the app to encourage them to refrain from using the scooter in a certain way. There are three levels of warnings: 

 

# *first warning* - informs the user about the risks of misbehavior; 
# *second warning* - limits the speed of the scooter until the overall user score improves; and 
# *third warning* - temporarily suspends the user from the service. The user is able to contest the suspension by contacting our Customer Support Team for further information as to why their account was suspended.

 

For safety considerations, we cannot disclose the exact thresholds that trigger our warnings to prevent users from abusing the system.
