It is true that contract conclusion occurs when the customer signs up for Bolt Business in the portal, there is no other way around it, and Special Terms that also form part of the contract are concluded on a “need to have” basis. This is because General Terms and Conditions that regulate the general relationship between the parties can change at any time if this will be required. We cannot sign General Terms and Conditions that will not change. However, we are allowing to introduce modifications to the terms set out in the General Terms and Conditions via Special Terms, which will prevail in case we make changes to the same provisions set out in the General Terms and Conditions. So technically, there is a contract “on paper”, but it just consists of several elements and one of the elements (General Terms) is available on our website.

** (1) Under this proposed arrangement, will GAC be processing Bolt employee data on EY’s behalf as a processor, or as an independent controller?
** (2) Are there any data processing / sharing agreements currently in place between EY and GAC that could cover GAC’s processing of Bolt employee data under this arrangement?
** (3) Will GAC be sharing Bolt employee data with any additional third parties?

+*Analysis*+

The only EY document that appears to contain explicit data privacy provisions is the _General Terms & Conditions_ (see Clauses 21-23). These Clauses identify EY as an independent controller of the personal data that Bolt will be sharing with them (this is fairly common in the case of professional service providers), and both parties seem to be based on Romania. As such, it is not legally mandatory for Bolt and EY to enter into any specific data processing / sharing terms in this case, and so {color:#36b37e}the EY agreement in of itself does not raise any obvious privacy issues{color}.

*However*, although not _legally mandatory_, there are a few things missing from the EY agreement that we would ordinarily push for. For example:

* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}does not make it clear exactly what types of personal data will be shared{color}, for what purposes, for how long etc. It is important to confirm this from an accountability perspective, given that we intend to share personal data with EY.
* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}could contain more explicit obligations requiring EY to keep Bolt employee data secure{color} (e.g., an obligation to ensure EY employees are properly trained when handling this data).
* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}does not require EY to indemnify Bolt for any breaches of data privacy law{color} concerning EY’s use of the personal data that will be shared by Bolt.

It is for these reasons (among others) that we ordinarily push for a more robust *data sharing agreement* to be in place when sharing personal data. I have taken the liberty of preparing a draft data sharing agreement (which can be found here: [LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/18k83eL5jluKdgbMlVRGRCKdk3h1WMeWvSDkQle4lMsg/edit]), which contains some comments for the attention of the EY team. Provided we have not previously entered into any sort of data sharing agreement with EY ({color:#4c9aff}*please confirm this point* {color}- I have not been able to find one on SpotDraft, but it is worth being sure), {color:#4c9aff}*I suggest providing this draft to EY*{color} in the first instance and seeing if they are amenable to it. If they are not, then we can make a business decision on whether it is worth pushing for any additional contractual protections.

Additionally, {color:#4c9aff}*it is worth confirming with the EY team how the sub-contractual relationship with GAC will work / be documented*{color} - in particular: (1) what role GAC will have when processing Bolt employee data (i.e., will GAC be acting as a controller or a processor?); and (2) what agreement / contractual protections will be in place between EY and GAC. Again, this is particularly important from an accountability perspective, as we need to ensure that any Bolt employee data that is passed on by EY to GAC is kept secured and processed in accordance with applicable privacy laws.

* We also need to be provided with some further information on how the sub-contractual relationship with GAC will work in practice, before we can sign-off on it from the privacy side. As such, *could you please ask EY the following*:
** (1) Under this proposed arrangement, will GAC be processing Bolt employee data on EY’s behalf as a processor, or as an independent controller?
** (2) Are there any data processing / sharing agreements currently in place between EY and GAC that could cover GAC’s processing of Bolt employee data under this arrangement?
** (3) Will GAC be sharing Bolt employee data with any additional third parties?
** (4) What is the full list of categories of personal data that will be shared by Bolt with EY (and subsequently, GAC) under this arrangement?

----

+*Analysis*+

The only EY document that appears to contain explicit data privacy provisions is the _General Terms & Conditions_ (see Clauses 21-23). These Clauses identify EY as an independent controller of the personal data that Bolt will be sharing with them (this is fairly common in the case of professional service providers), and both parties seem to be based on Romania. As such, it is not legally mandatory for Bolt and EY to enter into any specific data processing / sharing terms in this case, and so {color:#36b37e}the EY agreement in of itself does not raise any obvious privacy issues{color}.

*However*, although not _legally mandatory_, there are a few things missing from the EY agreement that we would ordinarily push for. For example:

* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}does not make it clear exactly what types of personal data will be shared{color}, for what purposes, for how long etc. It is important to confirm this from an accountability perspective, given that we intend to share personal data with EY.
* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}could contain more explicit obligations requiring EY to keep Bolt employee data secure{color} (e.g., an obligation to ensure EY employees are properly trained when handling this data).
* The EY agreement {color:#ff5630}does not require EY to indemnify Bolt for any breaches of data privacy law{color} concerning EY’s use of the personal data that will be shared by Bolt.

It is for these reasons (among others) that we ordinarily push for a more robust *data sharing agreement* to be in place when sharing personal data. I have taken the liberty of preparing a draft data sharing agreement (which can be found here: [LINK|https://docs.google.com/document/d/18k83eL5jluKdgbMlVRGRCKdk3h1WMeWvSDkQle4lMsg/edit]), which contains some comments for the attention of the EY team. Provided we have not previously entered into any sort of data sharing agreement with EY ({color:#4c9aff}*please confirm this point* {color}- I have not been able to find one on SpotDraft, but it is worth being sure), {color:#4c9aff}*I suggest providing this draft to EY*{color} in the first instance and seeing if they are amenable to it. If they are not, then we can make a business decision on whether it is worth pushing for any additional contractual protections.

Additionally, {color:#4c9aff}*it is worth confirming with the EY team how the sub-contractual relationship with GAC will work / be documented*{color} - in particular: (1) what role GAC will have when processing Bolt employee data (i.e., will GAC be acting as a controller or a processor?); and (2) what agreement / contractual protections will be in place between EY and GAC. Again, this is particularly important from an accountability perspective, as we need to ensure that any Bolt employee data that is passed on by EY to GAC is kept secured and processed in accordance with applicable privacy laws.

*section 28 (d)* You may provide a Journey by any reasonable route, and Bolt UK does not set any route restrictions. Please also refer to the Minimum Service Standards in respect of Journeys in Section 32.

*section 30(i)*You may complete a Journey by any reasonable route, and Bolt UK does not set any route restrictions. Please also refer to the Minimum Service Standards in respect of Journeys in Section 32.

+*PASSENGER TnCs*+ 

*Section 11*

g. You acknowledge that while receiving the Journey:

       i. the Driver can take any reasonable route to your requested destination;

       ii. you can amend your route in consultation with your Driver, in which case, your Fare can change;

* If we alter the current process, we will need to update both the driver and passenger Terms and Conditions. If the process changes to allow passengers to choose the route instead of the driver, and Bolt sends messages to drivers asking them to justify route deviations, this could be seen as a form of control over the driver's operations, potentially problematic for Employment Tribunal proceedings, as it doesn't align with the IC model.
* As long as drivers are not penalised for not accepting the passenger's preferred route, and the final price of the trip remains unchanged if the driver deviates from the rider-selected route, there should be no issues with rolling out this logic. This approach ensures that drivers do not overcharge passengers, improving user experience and likely reducing refunds. However, in cases where there are legitimate reasons for taking a different route, drivers should be compensated accordingly.

* AB to liaise with product legal to see if a global review has been conducted.

# _Does this mean that every passenger that books a ride will be given the option to choose the preferred route?_

# _Can the business meet its objectives by submitting trips for price review (ensuring the final price does not change) when overcharging occurs due to drivers intentionally taking significantly longer routes to increase fare prices? Hey!

Thank you for your patience!

This is one interesting topic as this can be region-specific. As a general approach, damage claims don’t need to have an invoice per se as covering the damages does not fall under goods nor services.

As usually, the damage claim consists of different components, then some of which might be considered service - but this subject should be discussed with a more knowledgeable person from the tax team.

Damage claim usually has supporting documents - like a sales invoice for the wreck/invoice for the repair services rendered, etc. And at the moment, there hasn’t been anyone contesting this approach. We had a similar question in EE regarding the basis documentation for payment (it was related to a contractual penalty) and as far as I remember, the accounting team told us this does not fall under their domain as this is not related to goods and services, rather it’s a contractual obligation and the contract itself can be the basis for submitting the claim (essentially: here are the terms you agreed to, here is the price list for penalties, here is the notification for payment - pay up!). 

In my opinion, if a third person wants to cover the damages, it should be okay as we’re okay with transferring the claim and we’re okay with a third person fulfilling the claim. 

Maybe the closest thing I can think of is a court decision. If a court orders you to pay the other party a sum, you don’t have a separate payment document for it - the decision itself is the grounds for the payment (and it’s done directly to the bank account). 

But yeah, coming back to the question - if a third person seals/hijacks our vehicle, we don’t have a contractual relationship with them and we can only present direct damage claims (extra-contractual damage), and the penalties are thus avoided.

# _From where the data will be collected?_

|[https://www.census.gov/naics/|https://www.census.gov/naics/|smart-link]|NAICS code|

*Suntec*: Logging into any social media or third-party accounts is not required to verify the given contact details. In your project, it seems that all the contact details are already available, so we just need to verify them.

# _You wouldn’t be overwhelming nor compromising any servers or service during scraping?_

*Suntec*: That’s correct. We are manually acquiring the required account & contact details from various online sources where data is publicly available, and it obeys to the terms and conditions of each website. # _What are your methods? Large-scale, high frequency? Would you be using automations?_

*Suntec*: Automation is certainly possible if the data needs to be scraped from any web directory where data points are very much in standard form. {noformat}select 
 count(co.id) as refunds_with_child_orders,
 count(*) as all_orders
from customer_support.support_case_refund_executed re
left join ng_delivery_spark.delivery_order_child_order co on re.order_id = co.parent_order_id 
where 
	date(re.created) between date('2024-01-01') and date('2024-07-15')
  and (action_type = 'delivery_original_payment_method_refund' or action_type  = 'delivery_bolt_balance_refund')
  and (re.assignee_user_id == 19039 OR re.assignee_user_id = 10030)
-- 1812/273453{noformat}

I.e. refunds where the final assignee was a bot.

Your converted query brings almost the same results:


{noformat} select    
 COUNT(CASE WHEN (re.assignee_user_id = 19039 OR re.assignee_user_id = 10030) AND co.id IS NOT NULL THEN re.support_case_id ELSE NULL END) AS refunds_with_child_orders,
  COUNT(sc.id) AS all_orders
from ng_customer_support_spark.etl_tw_support_case as sc
inner join customer_support.support_case_refund_executed re on sc.id = re.support_case_id
left join ng_delivery_spark.delivery_order_child_order co on re.order_id = co.parent_order_id
where

Hey! In the legislation of Ukraine there is no separate concept of a road accident with an animal, so such cases are equated to ordinary traffic accidents. For the guilty driver, this may result in a fine of UAH 340 (Article 124 of the Code of Criminal Procedure). In fact, the penalty for a hit-and-run involves only repairing driver’s own car. However, in the EU, the issue of accidents with animals is in the legal field, and insurance companies are responsible for compensation for such cases.

Anyway accident with animal is high priority case. And would be great to write it down for the agent to help them identify the issue.

Need to clarify whether or not the we will take into account *Delivery minimum price distance*. So the example in the description becomes

Then if we need to calculate the delivery fee for an order with distance of 5km *and a delivery minimum price distance of 2 km* 

Delivery fee *without minimum price distance (surchargeable distance 5km)* = Base Delivery Fee + Surcharge per km for range [0,2]* 2km + Surcharge per km for range [2,4]*2km + Surcharge per km for Range [4,Infinity]*1km = 1 + 0*2km+0.5*2km+1km*0.75 = 2.75 euros

Delivery fee *with minimum price distance (surchargeable distance 5km-2km=3km)* = Base Delivery Fee + Surcharge per km for range [0,2]* 2km + Surcharge per km for range [2,4]*1km = 1 + 0*2km+0.5*1km = 1.5 euros

Hello, good afternoon.

I fully agree that the cover of damages caused by a third party (i.e., the person who caused the damage or the person who’s legally liable for the actions taken by another person, like a son) does not qualify as a service or a transfer of goods for VAT purposes. Therefore, in principle, Bolt shall not charge VAT on the amount paid to cover the damages.

In broad terms (and in other words) indemnities to compensate damages and losses fall out of the scope of VAT, so we shall not charge VAT and we don’t have to support the payment of the indemnity with an invoice. A statement or a note should suffice.

On the other hand, if we don’t charge an indemnity to the person who pays for the damages, but we mean to pass through the cost of the repair services supplied by a third party, then the VAT approach to such a situation would be different. Under such a scenario, Bolt must issue an invoice to recharge the repair cost, and charge VAT.

In summary:

# Indemnities aimed at compensating Bolt from damages or losses fall out of the scope of VAT and do not have to be supported through an invoice. A statement would do.
# Repair costs passed through to the person who caused the damage fall within the scope of VAT, so in that case we must charge VAT to the payee through the corresponding invoice.

Thanks and have a nice day.

Hello Kjell,

Thank you for sharing your thoughts on how we can improve the feedback collection. I understand your point of view, but we depend on the workflow and resources we have. 

Talent LMS (Training Base) does not offer the option you are suggesting. We use it to upload our training content, but we don’t own this tool, so the improvements you are suggesting are not within our control. We can forward your suggestion to the Talent LMS platform, but it does not mean they will make this feature any time soon. We also cannot switch to a different tool, as Talent LMS offers a lot of the things we need and has been approved for its features and cost. 

When it comes to our feedback workflow, we have smaller groups formed from Subject Matter Experts who are assigned to review training material and leave feedback before any new training is published. A training designer then checks the comments, solves the feedback, and re-uploads the material in Talent LMS. We regularly review our onboarding. We also track all of the feedback that comes through the surveys in Talent LMS and via our Service Desk. 

To clarify a bit more, even if we had a feature you suggested, like Khan Academy and Codeacademy, we would not maybe use it for all of our learners. The reason is that our learners have a time constraint in which they have to do the training and we cannot expect them to leave feedback throughout the course as well, as it would take a lot of their time. Furthermore, not everyone provides correct actionable feedback and we need this sort of feedback, to be efficient with our time.

If you have more feedback on a specific training, and submitting it in a SD is not helping you, please let us know, and we will send you a training review link, where you can enter your feedback more easily. You mentioned the training materials are often outdated. I would appreciate it if you could be more specific about it. I will gladly fix something you spot as incorrect. There is only one training designer for each business line responsible for creating and updating all the materials, so help us help you. 😉 

P.S. All the feedback is centralised already, you don’t need to worry about that.

Decided to reject PR, which moves custom global A/B test logic into unified A/B test transformer [https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/104906|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/pull/104906|smart-link] 

Here is why:

After several attempts to make it work I think it is rather hard to migrate A/B test decision wrapper to unified global AB test Transformer.

{{user_rental_request}} checkpoint result consists of several components:

# decision
# pre-authorisation (includes severity, amount and currency)
# should_limit_ride_to_authorisation_amount

All these result components are computed based on triggered rules.
However, fuse and A/B test may (should be able to) override these components.
E.g. there is requirement to set should_limit_ride_to_authorisation_amount = false in case user is in treatment group of global A/B test. Also global A/B test resets pre-auth to 0.

It means that unified AB test transformer should return values for these components. But these components are specific for the {{user_rental_request}} checkpoint.
So, either unified AB test should know about specific fields for specific checkpoint and also be able to compute currency based on country (so, it should include locale dependency).
Or we should also support custom global AB test transformer (which is current implementation).

In previous PRs Johannes tried one more approach. He extracted pre-auth and should_limit logic into separate transformers (and put them after global A/B test transformer. Thus A/B test transformer doesn't need to return pre-auth and should_limit fields)
But I think it complicates the decision logic (e.g. pre-auth transformer should also know about results of A/B test).
Also it won't work correctly together with rules a/b test. Rules a/b test is executed the last. Rules a/b test removes 1 or several triggered rules and executes decision maker one more time. Decision maker doesn't include pre-auth and should_limit logic.

Conclusion:
Decided to reject this PR

Side note:
Seems, found a bug. Limit pre-auth A/B test doesn't take into account CHALLENGE decision. Should be fixed in separate PR

In summary, our thoughts on the most appropriate contractual approach from a privacy perspective is to do the following:

# *Amend the current DPA* to reflect that the fact that the personal data of end users in partner markets will now be processed under the new arrangement, as well as to reflect some other general amendments that we ordinarily push for in these types of agreement (we have prepared a revised draft to reflect this); +*and*+
# Require the partner market entities (“*PMEs*”) to enter into a separate *side letter* with Bolt, which requires the PMEs to comply with applicable data protection laws when using the tool and to indemnify Bolt as the licensee (we are engaging external counsel to prepare this side letter).

More detailed analysis on the reasoning behind these steps can be found below. Happy to discuss as needed! 🙂 

----

+*The Issues*+

The original request was whether we could just change the definition of ‘Customer’ to include ‘Customer’s Partners' in the DPA, to cater for the proposed arrangement with the PMEs. The issues with doing this and nothing else are as follows:

* It is mandatory that Exhibit A of the DPA sets out the details of the data processing that takes places under the DPA. This includes information on: (1) the categories of individuals whose personal data are processed; and (2) the categories of personal data that are processed. Under the new arrangement, Seismic will now also be processing the personal data of end users of the PMEs (i.e., an *additional category of individuals*), and based on discussions on this ticket we also understand that end users can provide personal data to Seismic to create content on the platform (i.e., *an additional category of personal data* not currently reflected in the DPA). In short, {color:#ff5630}*Exhibit A of the DPA likely does not currently contain all information needed to reflect the arrangement with the PMEs*{color}.
* We ordinarily push for various specific provisions in DPAs to ensure that Bolt’s position is protection (e.g., indemnities in favour of Bolt for any violations of data privacy laws). {color:#ff5630}*Many of these protections are not included in the Seismic DPA*{color}. We recently had external counsel review the Seismic DPA and flag specific issues / risk areas that are worth addressing in this regard.
* Under local data privacy laws of certain countries, you are not allowed to transfer any personal data out of the country unless you have put in place specific and mandatory contractual arrangements to ensure that the personal data is protected. For example, if you are transferring personal data out of the _European Union_, Bolt may be required to enter into a specific agreement called the ‘Standard Contractual Clauses’ - this is currently covered in the Seismic DPA. I understand that PMEs in Georgia, Saudi Arabia, Mexico, Hungary and Austria will be transferring personal data to the USA (i.e., Seismic) under the new arrangement. Although I am not an expert on data privacy laws in Saudi Arabia, Mexico and Georgia, if these countries impose a similar obligation to have a specific agreement in place covering the transfers, then {color:#ff5630}*such agreements / transfer arrangements are not covered in the Seismic DPA*{color}.

As such, to mitigate non-compliance risk and ensure that Bolt’s position is protected, should address the above issues as we enter into the new arrangement.

----

+*Solution (1) - Amendments to the DPA*+

To address the first two issues above, we have drafted some *amendments to the DPA* to: (1) cover the additional data processing details in Exhibit A; and (2) include provisions that we would typically want to see to protect Bolt’s position. The revised DPA can be found via the below link (edits are in ‘suggesting’ mode), and includes internal comments for your attention:

[https://docs.google.com/document/d/14x1maasFyiwnJ_YSdxtLPBxfx0uFX8eF/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/14x1maasFyiwnJ_YSdxtLPBxfx0uFX8eF/edit|smart-link] 

Next steps in this regard will be as follows:

# {color:#4c9aff}*Review the comments* {color}titled _NOTE TO BOLT LEGAL TEAM_ and address any questions / points we have raised.
# Once the questions have been addressed and the internal comments removed, we can {color:#4c9aff}*provide the proposed amendments to Seismic* {color}for their review and comments. When doing so, we can flag to Seismic that we will also be requiring the PMEs to enter into a separate side letter with Bolt, which we are currently preparing (see Solution (2) below).

----

+*Solution (2) - Side letter*+

To address the third issue above, *Bolt can enter into a separate side letter with the PMEs*. This side letter will do the following:

* Require the PMEs to comply with applicable data privacy laws when using Seismic’s services (including when submitting any personal data to the platform and exporting it out of their respective countries). The result of this would be that it would be up to the PMEs to enter into any additional DPAs / data transfer agreements to the extent required, depending on the laws of their country; 
* Include an indemnity given by the PMEs to Bolt as the licensee (to further protect Bolt’s position as a ‘middle man’ under the new arrangement).

Next steps in this regard will be as follows:

# {color:#4c9aff}*We (i.e., the privacy team) are today instructing Lighthouse to prepare a template of the side letter* {color}(as we intend to re-use it if similar situations like this arise going forward). We will keep you posted on developments and share it with you when it is ready.
# Once the side letter is ready, we can {color:#4c9aff}*provide it to the relevant PMEs to sign*{color}, and explain what additional actions they may need to take (e.g., entering any additional agreements on their side) so that they understand what may be required.

My reading of the Law is the following:

* The DL was published on 28.06.2024. 
* Article 2 amends article 16 of DL 1A/2020, which now determines the following: all documents with expiration date of 15.06.2024 or after will be valid until 30.06.2025. The expiration date does not change, it simple states the the documents are still considered/will still be accepted by public authorities until 30.06.2025. After 30.06.2025, the same documents (all documents with expiration date of 15.06.2024 or after) will still be valid if the owner shows proof of appointment to renew the documents. 
* This means i don’t necessarily agree with your second statement that: “Document expires before 2024-06-13 > Proof of renewal must be submitted before changing expiration date to 2025-06-30” as it is not what is stated in the law. 
* Therefore, i do agree with your first statement but regarding your second my reading is that documents with expiration date before 14.06.2024 are simply not valid. 
* The main question is, should we consider that documents that were considered valid until 2024-06-30 by the last amendment should be automatically extended to 2025-06-30? The answer would be no.

Hi [~accountid:624d3e6b699649006aea9c98] , I reviewed the document and I have one overarching question - why do we need these separate guidelines for data deletion? What is the goal from your side?

For some context, data deletion guidelines fall under the GDPR process, and, as we have to ensure GDPR compliance globally, we need to make sure that there are no deviations to our usual process. Additionally, in case we fail to implement GDPR properly due to failure of having a global, overarching process for data deletion requests management, we risk exposure to regulatory inquiries.

Some comments after reviewing the document you shared ([https://docs.google.com/document/d/10a88A5bLwiqnRuh1SG4PLZOOaMM1VgYjnTWRPSE2ht8/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/10a88A5bLwiqnRuh1SG4PLZOOaMM1VgYjnTWRPSE2ht8/edit|smart-link] ):

* we should refrain from making statements such as “the company does not delete data” or “we have no technical capability to delete data” - these statements are very sensitive in terms of GDPR, and could cause the company harm in case it’s shared with a broader audience/unauthorized persons/customers, i.e. drivers/passengers.
* we should remain in line with our KB guidelines on data deletion ([~accountid:641d5e830e6828ab20269e6d] will be able to support later on this) 



I am happy to discuss this further, however, I’d like to understand the reason we want to have these guidelines.

This may result in a scenario where, if a business customer deactivates and removes a business user's account, this individual will lose access to an alternative payment option (Bolt Business) and an additional ride category (Business Ride)._

_However, they will continue to be a customer of Bolt, which means Bolt will keep processing their personal data unless this individual decides to_ [_request_|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/data-subject/] _data deletion or the data retention period specified in_ [_Bolt`s privacy notices_|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/] _expires. In practical terms, this means that the personal data provided by business customers is used to match newly added business users with the accounts of standard users. Individuals remain in control over their data._

_Additionally, as there had been a contractual relationship with the business customer, the data received from the business customer may be required for solving any dispute that may arise from the agreement with the business client. Deleting personal data on the request of business customers may deprive both Bolt and the individual from the opportunity to defend or substantiate their claims in the event that any claims should arise. Therefore, the data will be stored by Bolt as a data controller for the above stated purposes unless this individual decides to_ [_request_|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/data-subject/] _data deletion or the data retention term provided by the law (limitation period for possible claims) expires, as outlined in the applicable_ [_Bolt`s privacy notices_|https://bolt.eu/en/privacy/]_._

_Please note that the notion of controllership in our arrangement is cemented by the_ [_EDPB Guidelines 07/2020_|https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-072020-concepts-controller-and-processor-gdpr_en] _on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. Specifically, p. 27 para. 82 demonstrates this via “Example: Taxi service”. While Bolt operates as an online platform rather than providing taxi services directly, the example still effectively clarifies the logic underpinning the controller relationship._

_We appreciate your attention and trust that this explanation has clarified any concerns or questions you may have._

*Summary of the Driver Queue Optimizer (DQO) feature (previously Availability Model)*
{panel}



*_Documentation part_*

* PPRA completed (see Cognito)
* DPIA completed and the DPO was consulted
** Here are the DPO’s comments on the DPIA: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ynnVO8L45iLZpR0UZyf0w4DrxsLI_GYu2VzHmrAar1Y/edit?usp=sharing|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ynnVO8L45iLZpR0UZyf0w4DrxsLI_GYu2VzHmrAar1Y/edit?usp=sharing|smart-link]



*_Considerations of DQO being automated decision-making_*

* From practical point of view, the problematic part was determining whether DQO can cause significant effect to the drivers. 
* To assess this, we requested the product team to help us document the fact that there is no significant effect to the drivers due to DQO being live.
** *Logic*: If we compare drivers A (no DQO) and drivers B (with DQO enabled) and we see that the loss of earnings due to being deprioritized is lower than X%, we can consider that the impact is not significant, because the losses are minor.
** This check is applied to all EU and other high-risk countries.
* The reason of having this check is - if we see that the effect DQO has on a driver is significant, we wouldn’t launch it in that country.



Feature was rolled out gradually, it is not live in all countries/cities, see the city list in this thread: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02CUF8CFCZ/p1708012487970579?thread_ts=1699019662.151329&cid=C02CUF8CFCZ|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02CUF8CFCZ/p1708012487970579?thread_ts=1699019662.151329&cid=C02CUF8CFCZ|smart-link]

Hey [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3] 

Drivers can be enrolled (start accepting Scheduled Rides) once they met the criteria, for example specific AR and DS thresholds,there are certain criteria configured for a given geographical area (can be set per country, but also per city). For all drivers, their "enrollment status" is calculated once every 24 hours. What that means is that their information is fetched and checked against the criteria, and if they pass all criteria they are enrolled, and if not they are unenrolled.

City-level configs override country level configs. So in this case, enrollment is disabled for the United Kingdom, but enabled in London, hence drivers are enrolled in London but not in the rest of the UK (unless that city also has a config that enables SR enrollment). 

And in London specifically, all drivers are enrolled, since the minimum driver score and acceptance rates are all set to 0, seems to be the same in Birmingham.

Meaning that, for London and Birmingham drivers can not be unenrolled.

Let me know if this helps.

Best,

Hi [~accountid:5e5cecb04befbd0c96cab72a],

I would like to seek your help, to test the 3WM rules, in BOLT2, and please report back your findings on what is happening. The rules have been setup both at header & line level, and you can find the relevant confluence link here: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/WDFTECH/pages/4803692732/3-Way+Match+Process#System-Configuration|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/WDFTECH/pages/4803692732/3-Way+Match+Process#System-Configuration|smart-link] . The aim here, is to test the overall logic, that is working as expected, provide suggestions where you think scenarios may not be covered, and I would like to further discuss with you the exception flow (who needs to take what action). 

You are able to find the match rules in the system by accessing task: *View Supplier Accounts Match Rule Set.* There is only one which is called Bolt 3-Way Match Rules. In each rule, it should be logical to follow that a rule is defined, that has a reason against it with a condition rule defined (logic that drives it).

The rules that we are expecting to test, and work based on current configuration:

||*Match Rule*||*Expected Outcome*||
|Total Invoice > Total PO (should include tax)|This rule should trigger, if you book the invoice with a value greater than the PO amount (latest version).|
|Invoice Tax > PO Tax|This rule should trigger, if the tax on the invoice is higher than the PO amount. Example, the line extended amount (non-tax) total is 100k. The invoice line amount matches 100k.
But on the PO it has 0% tax applied. On invoice, it has 20% tax applied.|
|Invoice Line Unit Cost > PO Line Unit Cost|If a unit cost on a booked invoice is higher than PO line, this rule should trigger. Example PO Line unit cost is $1 and the unit cost on invoice is $2. Please note: for services based POs/Invoices, this rule would NOT trigger.|
|Invoice Line Quantity > PO Line|If invoiced quantity > PO quantity then this rule should trigger. Example : on PO we have qty of 50, and on invoice we get 55.|
|Invoice Line Extended Amount > PO Line|If extended amount (both goods & services) is higher on invoice than on PO, then this should trigger. Example, on relevant PO line we have extended amount of 2000, and on invoice we have 3000.|
|Invoice Line : No Receipt|If a receipt has not been created for that said line (but PO & Invoice line are fine) then we expect this trigger.|
|Invoice Line > Receipt Line|if the amount that has been invoiced, is greater than corresponding invoice line then this should trigger. This should signify that whatever we received, we are expected to pay.|

Few notes and considerations:

# These rules have been setup by BNB for initial procurement deployment in 2022. I have made minor adjustments and formatting to ensure they are clear to follow. If you have feedback based on process, then please advise in this ticket.
# Overall the rules need to be in place for a good bases and exisiting process, however they will most likely we reviewed by the procurement team in near-future.
# Consider the 3-Way match aims to match 3 documents together: PO, Receipt & Invoice.

Remember that amount order, amount invoices, amount received is important. So, if we get invoiced for more than we received, but less than we ordered, then this should trigger an exception that we should not be paying for something we have not received. Additionally, if we get invoices LESS than what we received, then this should NOT trigger a rule in theory, as we are underpaying.. maybe a warning, but not a hard match exception rule.

Let me know your thoughts

From Commerce Legal I have no concerns with this. From Fin. Reg. side, also cashback to Bolt Balance is OK, as per the [Fin Reg Playbook|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AZ6R3pQcPhwHNTbSdXytaZeG3T1CvIgO0N50WP1DcK4/edit#heading=h.f450wgjydeax] in Confluence. 

However, I just want to make sure we do not give cashback for certain things, as the Card Schme Rules have limits on the things a customer can get a cashback for (or limits to what a Merchant can give cashback for). 

Cashback is generally allowed only for purchases of tangible goods, not for standalone services or intangible goods. For example, service-oriented merchants like consultants or professionals may not be authorized to offer cashback. 

Here in the EU, certain regulated products, such as pharmaceuticals, alcohol, and tobacco, may have restrictions on cashback offerings due to stringent control over sales and distribution. So I would like to avoid giving/offering cash back for these kind of products. 

Moreover, and as complement to the Card Scheme Rules, the PSD2 encourages measures to ensure the security of transactions, which may include limits on the amount of cashback dispensed to prevent misuse or fraud. I see there are some caps in the project description. Ideally there should be a limit to the number of cashbacks a customer can get. 

As far as we do not offer cashback for regulated products, and there is a limit on the cashback amount (and limit on how many cashbacks maybe as well) that a customer can receive, from Commerce Legal we are good.

*Summary:*

In Switzerland, Bolt wants to reach out to drivers with a promotion of a third party to help the drivers establish their own LLC and save money by paying less taxes. The exclusive offer would result in 15% discount.

It was flagged by the privacy function that promoting third party offers will require opt in consent from the drivers, as we are contacting them as individuals and not just B2B customers. As the stakeholder considers receiving opt in consent is problematic, an alternative approach was taken - to formulate the offer as coming from Bolt, and Bolt facilitating the set up of the limited liability company, and engaging a partner *(Fasoon)* to assist the driver with a discounted rate.

Specifically, it was framed in the following manner:

{quote}_Bolt is providing a commission reduction for drivers who set up their own companies to help minimise the cost of your work. To make this transition smoother, we have engaged a service provider Fasoon to offer assistance to our drivers throughout the process at a discounted rate._{quote}

This approach was taken and the comms were redone. The regulatory risk in Switzerland is generally medium (as advised by Fieldfisher), but considering  the nature of the offer, its target to drivers, and limited scope of data subjects (1100 drivers) - the risks were flagged as *low-medium.* Business took the decision to follow this approach and not rely on opt in consent.

Their response:

Bom dia, Afonso.

Agradecemos a vossa resposta e os esclarecimentos prestados. No entanto, gostaríamos de apresentar algumas considerações e pontos de discordância, bem como propor uma solução conjunta para avançarmos com a assinatura do contrato.

Na reunião assumimos que a responsabilidade autónoma para algumas finalidades poderia ser o caminho. Contudo, durante a mesma e considerando o modelo de negócio por vós apresentado, não podemos concordar plenamente com a posição assumida. Estamos, no entanto, dispostos a definir uma cláusula que acautela as finalidades próprias da Bolt e a subcontratação conforme as seguintes considerações:

* Conforme estabelecido nas Orientações EDPB 07/2020, na pág. 27, parágrafo 82, "_a mesma entidade pode agir na qualidade de responsável pelo tratamento em relação a determinadas operações de tratamento e, simultaneamente, na qualidade de subcontratante em relação a outras, pelo que a qualificação como responsável pelo tratamento ou como subcontratante tem de ser analisada face a conjuntos de dados ou operações específicos. (…) sempre que o serviço prestado não vise especificamente o tratamento de dados pessoais ou sempre que esse tratamento não constitua um elemento fundamental do serviço, o prestador do serviço pode estar em posição de determinar de forma independente as finalidades e os meios desse tratamento que é necessário para prestar o serviço_”.
* Nesse sentido, assumimos que no tratamento dos dados, nome e contacto telefónico, para a confirmação da identidade pelo motorista na recolha, assim como para a finalidade de gestão da qualidade do serviço, a Bolt desempenha efetivamente o papel de Responsável Autónomo pelo tratamento. No entanto, conforme mencionado no vosso email, estes dados são inseridos na plataforma com a finalidade de "_disponibilização de mensagem que permita ao passageiro seguir o motorista até ao seu ponto de recolha_", o que é diferente das finalidades de confirmação da identidade e gestão da qualidade do serviço. Foi-nos dito que na plataforma do motorista não aparecem dados de identificação do passageiro; necessitamos, portanto, que esclareçam se esses dados efetivamente aparecem para o motorista ou se são necessários exclusivamente para o envio da mensagem ao passageiro.
* Partindo do modelo de negócio explicado durante a reunião, entendemos que a Bolt irá disponibilizar uma plataforma fechada, com acesso exclusivo da Fidelidade Assistência, onde esta poderá gerir os seus pedidos, incluindo a escolha dos dados pessoais a serem inseridos. A Bolt não terá acesso a esses dados, e o cliente não precisará de ter a app da Bolt. Esta gestão será da exclusiva responsabilidade da Fidelidade Assistência, incluindo a definição das finalidades e dos meios.

*Gostaríamos de questionar novamente, atendendo a que não ficou claro na reunião:* +*Quais são as vossas finalidades próprias para o tratamento dos dados?*+

Considerando o interesse mútuo em avançar com o projeto, enviamos em anexo uma nova proposta, na expectativa que considerem a mesma.

Aguardamos a vossa resposta para que possamos concluir este processo de forma satisfatória para ambas as partes.

Thank you for your reply and clarifications. However, we would like to present some considerations and points of disagreement, as well as propose a joint solution to move forward with signing the contract.

At the meeting we assumed that autonomous responsibility for some purposes could be the way forward. However, during the meeting and considering the business model you presented, we cannot fully agree with the position you took. We are, however, willing to define a clause that safeguards Bolt's own purposes and subcontracting according to the following considerations:

As set out in EDPB Guidelines 07/2020, page 27, paragraph 82, “the same entity may act as controller in relation to certain processing operations and simultaneously as processor in relation to others, so qualification as controller or processor has to be examined against specific data sets or operations. (...) where the service provided does not specifically aim to process personal data or where such processing does not constitute a fundamental element of the service, the service provider may be in a position to independently determine the purposes and means of such processing as is necessary to provide the service.”

In this sense, we assume that in the processing of the data, name and telephone contact, for the confirmation of identity by the driver at the pick-up point, as well as for the purpose of managing the quality of the service, Bolt effectively plays the role of Autonomous Data Controller. However, as mentioned in your email, this data is entered into the platform for the purpose of “providing a message that allows the passenger to follow the driver to his pick-up point”, which is different from the purposes of confirming identity and managing the quality of the service. We have been told that no passenger identification data appears on the driver's platform; we therefore need clarification as to whether this data actually appears for the driver or whether it is needed exclusively to send the message to the passenger.
Based on the business model explained during the meeting, we understand that Bolt will provide a closed platform, with exclusive access for Fidelidade Assistência, where the latter can manage its requests, including the choice of personal data to be entered. Bolt will not have access to this data, and the customer will not need to have the Bolt app. This management will be the sole responsibility of Fidelidade Assistência, including the definition of purposes and means.
*We would like to ask again, since it was not clear at the meeting: What are your own purposes for processing the data?*

Considering the mutual interest in moving forward with the project, we are sending you a new proposal in the hope that you will consider it.

We look forward to your response so that we can conclude this process in a way that is satisfactory to both parties.





Thank you.

Hi, privacy team is working on this issue and will revert by early next week.

*Explanation:*

For *scheduled takeaway* orders, we use synthetic states in the app when it’s time to start preparing (states that don’t exist in the backend).

This is because the backend only supports transitioning from accepted → waiting for pickup, so we need to add fake UI-only intermediate states (waiting for prep confirmation, preparing).

OTOH ETA’s are cached in the polling service. Each cache entry lives for at most 6 hours. *Cache entries are refreshed when order state changes occur in the backend.* These state changes do happen for regular scheduled delivery orders but _do not_ happen for scheduled takeaway orders!
That means the ETA entries for takeaway orders are quite likely to expire, leading to this issue.

*Advice:*

The best solution might be to implement support for *parallel takeaway*, if possible, and *make the synthetic app-only states real*.

[https://taxify.atlassian.net/issues/DPX-2144|https://taxify.atlassian.net/issues/DPX-2144]

*Before checking alternatives, I urge us to not throw this opportunity away!* The synthetic app-only states are technical debt (at least in their current state).

*Alternatives:*

* Longer cache entry timeout (unlikely, since it was already increased 1h → 6h, we would be looking at 6h → N days).
* Ability to request ETA from the backend on-demand (while also refreshing the data in the polling cache?).
* ETA service could regularly refresh the ETA for scheduled takeaway orders.

UPDATE: order details also has an ETA value that should match the value from polling (which disappears).

After discussion with the privacy team, the following is information on the current data processing model in the partnership under discussion between Bolt and Fidelidade:

Bolt acts as an independent data controller when providing services to its business customers in all cases where the General Terms and Conditions for Bolt Business (“Bolt Business T&C”) apply. This includes, but is not limited to, Ride Booker services. 

Section 4 of the Bolt Business T&C explicitly states that Bolt and the business customer retain their independent roles of data controller for the processing of personal data. Bolt takes full responsibility for its processing activities and adherence to applicable laws, including the GDPR. This covers areas such as hiring sub-processors, implementing the necessary security measures and establishing data retention periods.

As for the potential uses of Ride Booker users' personal data, the main reason for Bolt to keep this personal data as a data controller is to safeguard Bolt against any dispute that may arise from the agreement with the business customer/Bolt business. Given that a contractual relationship has existed with the business customer, giving business customers the right to delete passengers' personal data may deprive both Bolt and the passenger of the opportunity to defend themselves or substantiate claims should any arise. Therefore, the data will be stored by Bolt as data controller for the above purposes, unless the passenger decides to request deletion of the data or the data retention period provided by law (limitation period for possible claims) expires, as described in the applicable Bolt privacy notices.

I also note that the notion of control in our agreement is cemented by the EDPB 07/2020 Guidelines on the concepts of controller and processor in the GDPR. Specifically, page 27, paragraph 82, demonstrates this through the “Example: Taxi service”. Although Bolt operates as an online platform rather than providing cab services directly, the example still effectively clarifies the logic behind the control relationship.

Therefore, the data protection clause in the Bolt Business terms and conditions should remain, and Bolt cannot accept the proposal in the special terms.  I hope this explanation clarifies the concerns raised at the last meeting.”

# Goods are ordered via procurement, and delivered to CWH. Goods are received and stocked. If ADR goods, then these may have to be placed with special rules for Health & Safety (BHP).
# Stock Requests are made to ship those goods out - when that is made, a packing list is generated to pick items, identify which items are ADR, put relevant sticker on shipment and packed pallet.
# When the shipment is booked via Cargoson platform, a button needs to be ticked, to signify it is ADR goods.
# Courier picks the goods up, and needs to be aware it is an ADR shipment he is carrying, and he is licensed and has the right machinery to operate that.
# When goods arrive at final destination, they may also be required to store ADR goods differently.

It is important to therefore ensure ALL parts of the ADR parts lifecycle can be automated, and risk can be reduced at every step - enabling the people to do better work and not have to worry about it.

We are going to develop two things, and we can make a decision as to which one is more suiting:

A) *Item Tag* - add an item tag to items, with a TRUE/FALSE whether an item is an ADR good.

B) *Purchase Item Group* - we could create a new PIG, and assign items there. This would therefore make it better for maintenance, and you would always have visibility as to what items are there.

We will be exploring both of these options, but it will be next week at the earliest due to capacities on current activities, and suggesting the options to you before deployment. This will require functional configuration, integration update, and potentially packing list layout change.

Vă mulțumim pentru solicitarea dvs. privind datele referitoare la mesajele trimise în legătură cu o călătorie efectuată la 23 iunie 2024.

După efectuarea unei căutări diligente a înregistrărilor referitoare la cererea dumneavoastră de acces, am confirmat că prelucrăm datele dumneavoastră cu caracter personal în contextul acestor mesaje. Legislația privind protecția datelor permite persoanelor fizice să obțină o copie a datelor lor cu caracter personal care fac obiectul căutării - adică date cu caracter personal care le identifică sau le permit să fie identificate pe baza acestora ca persoane fizice în viață.

După cum probabil știți, dreptul de acces în temeiul legislației privind protecția datelor nu oferă unei persoane un drept absolut de acces deplin la toate documentele care conțin datele sale cu caracter personal. De exemplu, legea impune unui operator de date precum noi să protejeze drepturile părților terțe. ❓ Firstly, I have the following *questions*:❓ 

* Are we exclusively considering whether the change to the CS process can be rolled out in Germany? Or would the process also be changed in other countries?
* When we talk about ‘fleet owners’ here, are we talking about _traditional_ fleet owners (i.e., the drivers are employees of the fleets) or _non-traditional_ fleet owners (e.g., in the case of car rental companies)? Or both?
* Why do fleet owners typically request to change a driver’s account details? If this because: (1) the fleet owner wants to update any inaccurate / out-of-date information; (2) the fleet owner is subject to a particular legal obligation to do so; or (3) another reason?
* Do we know whether fleet owners typically have any general authorisation from their drivers (in writing) to change their account details as they see fit?
* What types of information are included in the category of ‘a driver’s account details'? Presumably this includes name, email, ID, phone and bank account data - what else?



Subject to your responses to the questions above, I would advise {color:#ff5630}*keeping the CS process as it currently is*{color} (i.e., continue to require the fleet owners to provide us with a driver’s consent before we change the driver’s account details). This is because:

* The majority of information that comprises a driver’s account details will be their personal data (i.e., data that can be used to identify that specific driver). This information is being processed by Bolt (as the account is created on the Bolt platform). As such, Bolt is subject to data privacy laws (in particular, the GDPR) regarding how it can handle the majority of a driver’s account details.
* A request for Bolt to change a driver’s account details may count as a *rectification request* under the GDPR (i.e., a request to correct an individual’s personal data). In order for Bolt to be able to action such a request (i.e., change the account details), the request needs to come from either:
** (a) the individual whose personal data will be changed under the request (i.e., the driver); or
** (b) a third party that has been authorised by this individual to make the request on their behalf (i.e., a fleet owner that can provide proof of the driver’s consent - {color:#4c9aff}+*this is the rationale behind the current CS process*+{color}. Bolt needs to verify that the fleet owner has proper authority before Bolt can respond to a request on a driver’s behalf).
* In some circumstances, unauthorised alteration of an individual’s personal data (e.g., Bolt changing a driver’s account details without proper authorisation from the driver) may also count as a *personal data breach*. We need to take proportionate steps to avoid this.
* Finally, from a data security perspective, obtaining the driver’s consent to changing their personal data allows us to demonstrate that Bolt has appropriate security measures in place to protect such data, should we ever be challenged on this by a regulator.



As a final point, *I would not rely on ChatGPT’s advice* on this issue, particularly as we do not consider drivers as ‘employees’ of Bolt (and so a driver’s phone would not be a ‘work tool’ for present purposes). Happy to discuss if any of this is unclear 🙂

It is just not implemented for applepay/googlepay payment methods.

In order to implement it:

* check if {{`taxify_fraud`.`failed_pre_auth`}} table contains {{applepay/googlepay}} rows
* add index {{`taxify_fraud`.`failed_pre_auth`}} by user_id and payment_method_type
* implement query/endpoint which counts number of failed auth by these payment methods (similar to {{/internal/fraud/payment/getCardPaymentStats}} )
* add this data to checkpoint
* modify rule to use card payment stats together with mobile_payment_stats
